content: The analysis included 16,495 patients across multiple treatment arms. The results of the fixed-effects network meta-analysis (NMA) for the comparisons of interest are presented in the referenced sections. At 48 weeks, the reduced dose of efavirenz (EFV400) was not statistically distinguishable from the standard dose of efavirenz. The analysis of viral suppression at 144 weeks was based on data from six trials involving 13 treatment arms and 5,274 patients. However, EFV400 was not available at this time point, and the results of the fixed-effects NMA for viral suppression at 144 weeks are only partially presented. Dolutegravir (DTG) continued to demonstrate superior viral suppression, although only half of the comparisons were statistically significant, likely due to the smaller number of trials and patients. The evidence network for changes in CD4 cell counts at 48 weeks was based on 44 trials with 94 treatment arms, including 23,789 patients. Both DTG and EFV400 showed higher estimated increases in CD4 counts compared to most other treatments, though these differences were not statistically significant. At 96 weeks, the evidence network included 22 trials with 47 treatment arms and 15,134 patients. Results at this time point were similar to those at 48 weeks, indicating sustained improvement in CD4 counts over the second year. At 144 weeks, the evidence network included seven trials with 15 treatment arms and 7,019 patients. However, the network was sparse, and EFV400 was not available for analysis at this time point. The evidence base for mortality in first-line treatment included 21,604 patients across 29 trials with 62 treatment arms. Although mortality was considered a critical outcome, the trials were underpowered for this endpoint, with only 391 deaths reported. Many comparisons had zero events, making estimates unreliable. For example, only five deaths were reported in both the DTG and EFV400 groups. There were no statistically significant differences in mortality outcomes between DTG, EFV, and EFV400. The evidence base for AIDS-defining illnesses (ADIs) included 9,722 patients across 18 trials with 40 treatment arms. Similar to mortality, the analysis of ADIs was limited by a small number of events, with no statistically significant differences observed between treatments. For example, no ADIs were reported in several trials involving EFV. The evidence base for all-cause discontinuations (retention) included 26,399 patients across 120 treatment arms in 54 trials. DTG was statistically superior to most other treatments in terms of lower discontinuation rates, except for comparisons with EVG/c, BIC, and DOR. The comparison between DTG and EFV400 was based only on indirect evidence, with DTG appearing superior. For discontinuations due to adverse events, both DTG and EFV400 had the lowest odds and were superior to standard-dose EFV, though they were not statistically distinguishable from each other. The evidence for treatment-related adverse events included 15,599 patients across 61 treatment arms in 27 trials, while treatment-emergent adverse events included 18,915 patients across 70 treatment arms in 32 trials. DTG and EFV400 had lower odds of treatment-related adverse events compared to most other treatments, with DTG showing slightly better odds than EFV400. Bictegravir (BIC) had the lowest odds overall, followed by doravirine (DOR) and darunavir/ritonavir (DRV/r). The evidence for treatment-related serious adverse events (SAEs) was based on 8,041 patients across 31 treatment arms in 15 trials, while treatment-emergent SAEs included 26,706 patients across 98 treatment arms in 45 trials. Due to the small number of treatment-related SAEs (81 events), reliable estimates could not be obtained. However, treatment-emergent SAEs did not show the same limitations, and neither DTG nor EFV400 distinguished themselves from EFV, though their estimates were lower. The evidence base for regimen substitutions by 48 weeks included 9,263 patients across 41 treatment arms in 18 trials. Results indicated that regimen substitutions were less common with DTG compared to EFV in practice, though there was no direct evidence supporting the DTG-to-EFV comparison. Observed regimen substitutions were rare in the trials. GRADE assessments indicated high-quality evidence for improved viral suppression and lower discontinuations due to adverse events for DTG compared to EFV. Moderate-quality evidence supported improvements in CD4 counts and reductions in treatment-related adverse events. However, evidence for long-term efficacy at 144 weeks, mortality, ADIs, SAEs, and regimen substitutions was of low to very low quality due to imprecise estimates and a high risk of bias. For EFV400 compared to standard-dose EFV, high-quality evidence was available for discontinuations due to adverse events, while other outcomes were supported by moderate-quality evidence. Comparisons between DTG and EFV400 were limited to moderate-quality evidence for fewer discontinuations and better long-term viral suppression with DTG. For HIV-TB co-infected patients, evidence was limited. The interim analysis of the INSPIRING trial, which compared DTG and EFV in patients receiving rifampin-based TB therapy, showed that DTG led to relative increases in CD4 counts but was not distinguishable from EFV in terms of viral suppression. Safety and tolerability data were based on very few events. The systematic review identified 10 studies, but only six randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with 1,378 patients were included in the analysis. The evidence was limited to five treatments (NVP, DTG, EFV, and RAL at two doses), with no data available for EFV400. DTG was associated with significant increases in CD4 counts compared to other treatments, but no other comparisons were statistically significant.
